la:verb:declino.gloss: to bend, deviate, turn aside/away, deflect
senses: to bend, deviate, turn aside/away, deflect
la:verb:declino.html:
dē-clīno, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n.
CLINO = κλίνω
, orig.
to bend from the straight path; to turn aside or away (freq. and class.).
Lit.
Act.: ego modo declinavi paullum me extra viam,; cf.: sese rectā regione viai,; and: se a terris omnia numina, Poët. ap. : lumina, Catull. 64, 91: agmen,; : nares in alteram partem,.—Poet. of the eyes, to bend down, i. e. to lower, close them in sleep: nec dulci declinat lumina somno, * .—
Neutr.: paulum ad dexteram de via declinavi, ut ad Pericli sepulcrum accederem,; ; .—So of the oblique motion of atoms (corresp. with oblique ferri): si omnes atomi declinabunt, nullae umquam cohaerescent; sive aliae declinabunt, aliae suo nutu recte ferentur, etc.,; cf. (preceded by cur Epicurus atomos de via deducat): quae nova causa in natura est, qua declinet atomus? 20, 46 (the reading quae declinet atomum is wrong),.—
Trop.
In gen.
Act., to turn aside: neque (mulierem) declinatam quicquam ab aliarum ingenio ullam reperias, who has departed, deviated, * ; cf.: quaedam verborum flgurae paulum figuris sententiarum declinantur,; : neque spe, neque metu declinatus animus,: Cato literas Graecas aetate jam declinata didicit,in the decline of life,. —
Neutr., to turn aside, deviate, turn away: de via,; cf.: de statu suo,: a religione officii,: a malis (opp. appetere bona),: a parvis delictis diligentius,: aliquantulum a proposito,: a recto itinere (oratio),: gemma paulum declinans a topazio in aurum,passing,: ut eo revocetur unde huc declinavit oratio,digressed,; cf. : quantum in Italiam declinaverat belli,: in asperam Pholoen,: in pejus,: ad discendum jus,; cf. .—Absol.: declinasse me paululum et praesentes fluctus fugisse,: paulatim amor,decreases,: dies coeperat declinare,. —
In partic. grammat. t. t., to vary, inflect a part of speech.
In the older grammarians, of every kind of inflection (declension, conjugation, comparison, derivation, etc.), ; sq.; cf. also ; —
In the later grammarians, to decline, in the strict sense, Charis, p. 8 sq. et al. —
Transf., with an object denoting that from which one turns aside; to avoid, to shun (classical, most freq. in Cic.); nec satis recte (oratio) declinat impetum, nisi etiam in cedendo quid deceat intellegit,; cf., corresp. with vitare,, D. fin.; and: ictum,: urbem,: laqueos judicii,: appetuntur quae secundum naturam sunt, declinantur contraria,: vitia,: ea quae nocitura videantur,; cf. : invidiam,; : impudicitiam uxoris,: oppida ut busta,.
la:verb:declino.inflection: āvi, ātum, 1, v. a. and n.

senses: every change of a word; declension, conjugation, comparation, derivation etc.
la:noun:declinatio.html:
dēclīnātĭo, ōnis, f.
id.
,
a bending from a thing, a bending aside; an oblique inclination or direction (good prose).
Lit.: lanceam exigua corporis declinatione vitare,; cf.: quot ego tuas petitiones parva quadam declinatione effugi,: declinare dixit (Epicurus) atomum perpaulum, et ipsa declinatio ad libidinem fingitur, etc.,; so of the oblique motion of atoms, ; .—
Like the Gr. κλίμα, the supposed slope of the earth towards the poles, a region of the earth or sky, a climate: declinatio mundi, prooem. § 22; so, mundi,; cf.: positio caeli et declinatio,; so correspond. with regio caeli,; cf. also caeli,the altitude of the pole,.—
Trop.
In gen., a turning away from any thing; an avoiding, avoidance: ut bona natura appetimus, sic a malis natura declinamus; quae declinatio, si cum ratione fiet, cautio appelletur,; cf. so opp. appetitio,; and in plur. : laboris, periculi,—
t. t.
Of rhetor. lang., a short digression: declinatio brevis a proposito, non ut superior illa digressio,; ; cf. and 34.—
Of gramm. lang.: variation, inflection.
In the older grammarians, every change of form which a word undergoes; as declension, strictly so called, conjugation, comparison, derivation, etc., ; sq.; ; cf. also of declension in its stricter sense,; ; of conjugation,; of derivation,; .—
Among the later grammarians, of declension, properly so called, as distinguished from conjugatio, comparatio, derivatio, etc. So, Donatus: in declinatione compositivorum nominum, p. 174 P. (p. 13 Lind.).

la:verb:decerno.gloss: to decide, decide upon, settle, determine (especially something disputed or doubtful)
senses: to decide, decide upon, settle, determine (especially something disputed or doubtful)
to pronounce a decision concerning something; decide, determine, judge, declare, decree; vote for something
to decide by combat; fight, combat, contend
la:verb:decerno.html:
dē-cerno, crēvi, crētum, 3 (the syncop. forms decreram, etc., decrerim, etc., decresse are freq. in Cicero and Liv., also ; ; , but not in Caes., where is only decreverat, B. G. 4, 17; 5, 5
fin.; 5, 53, 2), v. a. and n.
(acc. to cerno, no. II. 3.) To decide, determine any thing disputed or doubtful. For syn. cf.: scisco, jubeo, statuo, constituo, dico, sancio, consilium capio, destino, obstino, definio, determino.
Prop., of a judge, magistrate, etc., to pronounce a decision respecting something; to decide, judge, determine, decree; to vote for any thing (very freq. and class.).—Const. with acc., with acc. et inf., a relat. clause, with de, or absol.: alias (Verres praetor) revocabat eos, inter quos jam decreverat decretumque mutabat, alias, etc.,: si quod est admissum facinus, si caedes facta, idem (Druides) decernunt,: consules de consilii sententia decreverunt secundum Buthrotios,, C, § 11: decernere vindicias secundum servitutem, in favor of slavery, i. e. restore the slave to his master, ; cf. : cum senatus triumphum Africano decerneret,; cf. of a single senator: non decrevi solum, sed etiam ut vos decerneretis laboravi,; so supplicationem decernere,; so also: Crassus tres legatos decernit,: D. Junius silanus supplicium sumendum decreverat,: quando id bellum senatus decrevisset, quando id bellum populus R. jussisset?; ; ; : id quod senatus me auctore decrevit,; : qui ordo decrevit invitus,on compulsion,: Ligures ambobus consulibus decernuntur,; cf.: provinciam desponsam non decretam habere, (v. the whole passage in connection): provinciae privatis decernuntur, et saep.: ex annuo sumptu, qui mihi decretus esset, et saep.: mea virtute atque diligentia perditorum hominum patefactam esse conjurationem decrevistis,: cum pontifices decressent ita; SI, etc.,: senatus decrevit populusque jussit, ut, etc.,: in jure dicundo, ita decrevit, ut, etc., ; cf. of individuals: Hortensii et mea et Luculli sententia ... tibi decernit, ut regem reducas, etc.,.—Impers.: in parricidas rei publicae decretum esse,.—Esp. of the emperor, to determine the law by deciding a case: quodcumque imperator cognoscens decrevit, legem esse constat,; .
Transf., beyond the judicial sphere, to decide, determine, judge: qui nequeas nostrorum uter sit Amphitruo decernere, Plaut. fragm. ap. : rem dubiam decrevit vox opportune emissa,; cf.: primus clamor atque impetus rem decrevit,; : de his Catonis praecepta decernent,: duo talenta pro re nostra ego esse decrevi satis,; : quam decrerim me non posse diutius habere,: in quo omnia mea posita esse decrevi,; : illum decrerunt dignum, suos cui liberos committerent,: in ejus controversiis quid decernas, non a te peto,: aliquem decernere hostem, to proclaim one an enemy by a formal decree, .—Absol.: nequeo satis decernere,.
Milit., to decide by combat; hence (like cernere and certare), in gen., to fight, combat, contend: castra castris conferamus, et Samnis Romanusne imperio Italiam regant, decernamus,; : in ipso illo gladiatorio vitae certamine, quod ferro decernitur,: proelium,: pugnam,; cf. : de bello decernere, Auct. B. Hisp. 5 fin. Oud. N. cr.: ne armis decernatur,; cf.: ferro ancipiti decernunt,: and armis, ferro,; 12, 282; 695 (cf. et cernere ferro, ): cursibus et crudo caestu,: cornibus inter se,: lapidibus et subselliorum fragminibus, et saep.: contra magnam vim hostium, artificio magis quam viribus, Auct. B. Afr. 14: acie,; : proelio cum proditore,: classe decreturi,: integriore exercitu,fin.—Absol.: decernendi potestatem Pompeio fecit,; cf. .
Transf., beyond the milit. sphere: decernite criminibus, mox ferro decreturi,—So of a judicial contest: uno judicio de fortunis omnibus decernit,; cf. ; and qui judicio decernent,: de salute reipublicae,: pro mea omni fama fortunisque,: utinam meo solum capite decernerem,; .
With reference to one's own acts, to decide, determine on doing something; to determine, resolve on something (freq. in all periods and styles).—Constr., with inf. and with acc. and inf.: si tu fluctus e gurgite tollere decreris, Lucil. ap. Rufin. § 26 (p. 238 ed. Frotsch.): quicquid peperisset decreverunt tollere,: Caesar his de causis Rhenum transire decreverat, et saep.: eos me decretum est persequi mores patris,; ; ; cf.: certum atque decretum est non dare signum,: reliquam aetatem a republica procul habendam decrevi,. With ut and subjunct.: hic decernit ut miser sit,.—With accus.: quicquam decernere,—Hence, dē-crētum, i, n.
(Acc. to no. I. A.) A decree, decision, ordinance of any political or judicial body (for syn. cf.: scitum, edictum, consilium, jus): senatus Caelium ab rep. removendum censuit. Hoc decreto eum consul senatu prohibuit,: si qui eorum (sc. Druidum) decreto non stetit, sacrificiis interdicunt,; cf. § 10: vestra responsa atque decreta evertuntur saepe dicendo,; : decurionum, et saep.: Caesaris,.—Esp. leg. t. t., a decision of the emperor as judge, a precedent (cf. rescriptum), ; .—
Transf., in philos. lang. as a translation of the Gr. δόγμα, principle, doctrine, precept, ; § 29; cf. and 95, 9 sq. (quis philoso, phorum) decretis suis paret? .

la:verb:decresco.gloss: to grow less or shorter, decrease, wane, dwindle
senses: to grow less or shorter, decrease, wane, dwindle
to vanish, fade, disappear, pass away by diminution
la:verb:decresco.html:
dē-cresco, crēvi, crētum, 3, v. n.
Orig., to grow less, grow shorter, decrease, wane (as the moon, bodies of water, the length of the day, etc.): ostreae cum luna pariter crescunt pariterque decrescunt, * : crescunt loca decrescentibus undis,; cf.: aequora,; and: decrescentia flumina, * : die decrescente (coupled with quo rursus crescente),: ubi febris fuit atque decrevit,; cf.: morbus, al.: nocte dieque decretum et auctum, Laev. ap. P.; of the waters of the flood,.—Hence,
In gen., to decrease, become less, diminish: uncus aratri Ferreus occulte decrescit in arvis,i. e. wears away,; ; ; : admiratio decrescit,: metus matrum, et saep.: ut corpora quamlibet ardua et excelsa, procerioribus admota decrescant,i. e. seem smaller,: decrescente reditu (agelli) etiam pretium minuit,.—
Poet., of the gradual disappearance of places as one removes farther from them, ; .—*
Pregn., to pass away by diminution; to vanish, disappear: cornua decrescunt, etc.,.

la:num:decimus.gloss: tenth; the ordinal number after nonus and before undecimus
senses: tenth; the ordinal number after nonus and before undecimus
la:num:decimus.html:
dĕcĭmus or dĕcŭmus (the latter form prevailed in the later law lang.; hence, decumanus), a, um, adj.
decem with superl. ending
,
the tenth.
Prop.: mensis,; cf. : legio,; cf. ; : decima hora,; and without hora,: annus,: septuma (dies) post decumam,i. e. the seventeenth, Voss.: cum decumo efficit ager,i. e. tenfold,; so, extulisset, ib. § 113.—*
dĕcĭmum, adv. (like tertium, quartum, etc.; cf. ), for the tenth time, .—
Subst.: dĕcĭma (dĕcŭma), ae, f. (sc. pars), the tenth part, tithe.
As an offering: testatur Terentius Varro ... majores solitos decimam Herculi vovere,; so Müll.; ; cf. with pars; Naev. ap. P.; : tibi (sc. Pythico Apollini) hinc decumam partem praedae voveo,; cf.: cum vovissent Apollini decumas praedae,; cf. ; ; so esp. of the tithes given by the Hebrews to support the priesthood, et saep.—
A largess openly bestowed by public men on the people: Oresti nuper prandia in semitis decumae nomine magno honori fuerunt,; so ; ; .—
A tithe, as a tax on landholders in the provinces, ; more freq. in plur., , § 89 sq.—
A tithe, as conveyed by last will: decimas uxoribus dari, Trach. ap. .
Meton. (like decem, decies, etc.), considerable, large, immense (poet.): vastius insurgens decimae ruit impetus undae, (cf.: decimanus, no. II., and in Gr. τρικυμία); so of billows,; ; (decimus by circumlocut.: qui venit hic fluctus, fluctus supereminet omnes; posterior nono est undecimoque prior,).

la:verb:decimo.gloss: to decimate (select every tenth person for punishment)
senses: to decimate (select every tenth person for punishment)
la:verb:decimo.html:
dĕcĭmo or dĕcŭmo, āvi, ātum, 1, v. a.
decimus
.
To select by lot every tenth man for punishment, to decimate (postAug., although the practice itself occurs as early as 283 A. U. C.; v. ), : cohortes,: cohortium militem, 4, 1, 37 al.— Absol., .—
To cause to pay tithes, to collect tithes from a person. —Pass.: et Levi decimatus est,.—
To select the tenth part as an offering, to pay tithes of anything, Müll.; .—Hence, dĕcŭmātus, a, um, P. a., selected, excellent, choice: honestas, and 51.—Sup.: juvenis,.

la:num:decem.html:
dĕcem (DEKEM, Corp. Inscr. Lat. 1, 844 al.—The best MSS. and editt. vacillate often between the word and its sign X),
num. [Sanscr. and Zend, daçan, Gr. δέκα, Old H. Germ. zëhan, Germ. zehn, Eng. ten], ten.
Prop.: decem minae, and 58: hominum milia decem,; : fundi decem et tres,; cf. : milia passuum decem novem,; .—
Decem primi (separated thus in the inscrr.), or in one word, Dĕcemprīmi, ōrum, m., the heads or presidents of the ten decuriae which usually formed the senate in an Italian city or Roman colony (afterwards called decaproti, v. h. v.): magistratus et decem primi,; ; and 1848. Their dignity was termed dĕcem-prīmātus, ūs, m. (also decaprotia, v. h. v.), .—
Meton., for an indefinite, round number: si decem habeas linguas, mutum esse addecet,; ; : habebat saepe ducentos, Saepe decem servos, etc.,: cf.: decies.

la:noun:decima.html:
dĕcĭma, ae, f., v. decimus,
no. I. B. and II. B.

la:verb:decipio.gloss: to catch, ensnare, entrap, deceive, mislead, beguile, elude, cheat
senses: to catch, ensnare, entrap, deceive, mislead, beguile, elude, cheat
la:verb:decipio.html:
dē-cĭpĭo, cēpi, ceptum, 3, v. a.
capio
, primarily signifies to catch away, catch up, seize an animal while running, fleeing, etc. (whence decipula, a snare, trap); but occurs only in the trop. sense (acc. to capio,
no. II. B.), to catch, ensnare, entrap, beguile, elude, deceive, cheat (for syn. cf.: fraudo, emungo, circumscribo, circumvenio, frustror, verba do, impono, fallo): fiunt transennae ubi decipiuntur dolis, etc.,: ita decipiemus fovea lenonem Lycum,; et saep.: eo deceptum, quod neque, etc.,: T. Roscius novem homines honestissimos ... induxit, decepit, omni fraude et perfidia fefellit,; cf.: illa amphibolia, quae Croesum decepit, vel Chrysippum potuisset fallere,; : homines imperitos et per colloquium deceptos crudelissime interfecisse, Caes. B. C. 1, 85, 3; so per aliquid,fin.; : in nullo verbo eum memoria decepit,. Praef. 18: jam semel in prima spe deceptos,; for which spe affinitatis deceptum,; cf.: deceptus nocte,: cupidine falso,: specie recti, et saep.: amatorem amicae decipiunt vitia,.—Poet., in Gr. construction: Prometheus dulci laborum decipitur sono, is beguiled of his sufferings (i. e. forgets his sufferings, being beguiled with sweet melody), .—
Of inanimate objects: exspectationibus decipiendis,; cf.: quo opinio decipitur,: oculos,; cf. : nervos,: volatile pecus facile custodiam pastoris decipit,: judicium error,: specimen istud virtutis,: sic tamen absumo decipioque diem,; cf. Loers.; ; : quomodo vinum potantem decipit,.—
Absol.: victima deceptus decipientis ero,: ab tergo et super caput decepere insidiae,; .

la:verb:decedo.gloss: to withdraw, retire, depart, leave or go away
senses: to withdraw, retire, depart, leave or go away
to desert or abandon, give up, resign, forego; yield
to yield, make way, step aside
la:verb:decedo.html:
dē-cēdo, cessi, cessum, 3 (
inf. sync. decesse, ; ; Neue Formenl. 2, 536. The part. perf. decessus perh. only ), v. n., to go away, depart, withdraw. (For syn. cf.: linquo, relinquo, desero, destituo, deficio, discedo, excedo. Often opp. to accedo, maneo; freq. and class.)—Constr. absol. with de, ex, or merely the abl.; rarely with ab.
Lit.
In gen.: decedamus,: de altera parte (agri) decedere,: decedit ex Gallia Romam Naevius,: e pastu,; cf.: e pastu decedere campis,: ex aequore domum,; Italiā,: Numidiā,: Africā,; 23, 1: pugnā,: praesidio, (cf.: de praesidio,): quae naves paullulum suo cursu decesserint,i. e. had gone out of their course,; so, cum luminibus exstinctis decessisset viā,had gone out of the way,: pantherae constituisse dicuntur in Cariam ex nostra provincia decedere,.
Esp.
t. t.
In milit. lang., to retire, withdraw from a former position: qui nisi decedat atque exercitum deducat ex his regionibus,; so,absol.,fin.; : de colle,: de vallo,: inde,: loco superiore,; so with abl., Auct. B. Alex. 34; 35 (twice); 70 al.—
In official lang.: de provincia, ex provincia, provinciā, or absol. (cf. ), to retire from the province on the expiration of a term of office: de provincia decessit,; so,; (twice); Drak.: decedens ex Syria,; so, e Cilicia,: ex Africa,: ex Asia,: ex ea provincia, Zumpt N. cr.: ut decedens Considius provinciā,; ; : te antea, quam tibi successum esset, decessurum fuisse,; so absol., : Albinus Romam decessit,; cf.: Romam ad triumphum,; . —Rarely with a: cui cum respondissem, me a provincia decedere: etiam mehercule, inquit, ut opinor, ex Africa,
Decedere de viā; also viā, in viā alicui, alicui, or absol., to get out of the way, to give place, make way for one (as a mark of respect or of abhorrence): concedite atque abscedite omnes: de via decedite,; cf.: decedam ego illi de via, de semita, (.

163; cf. II. B infra); cf.: qui fecit servo currenti in viā decesse populum,: censorem L. Plancum via sibi decedere aedilis coegit,; cf. : sanctis divis, Catul. 62, 268: nocti,: peritis, (cf.: cedere nocti,).—Also, to get out of the way of, avoid: decedere canibus de via,; cf.: hi numero impiorum habentur, his omnes decedunt, aditum defugiunt, etc.,.—By zeugma, in the pass.: salutari, appeti, decedi, assurgi, deduci, reduci, etc.,.

Pregn., to depart, disappear (cf.: cedo, concedo).
Of living beings, to decease, to die: si eos, qui jam de vita decesserunt,: vitā,; Mac. 6, 31; but commonly absol.: pater nobis decessit a. d. VIII. Kal. Dec.,: cum paterfamiliae decessit,; , and 3; ; ; ; ; et saep.: cruditate contracta,: morbo aquae intercutis,: paralysi,: ex ingratorum hominum conspectu morte decedere,.—
Of inanimate things, to depart, go off; to abate, subside, cease: corpore febres,: febres,; ; cf.: quartana, (opp. accedere): decessisse inde aquam,run off, fallen,; cf.: decedere aestum,; : de summa nihil decedet,to be wanting, to fail,; ; cf.: quicquid libertati plebis caveretur, id suis decedere opibus credebant,: decedet jam ira haec, etsi merito iratus est, (for which : cito ab eo haec ira abscedet): postquam invidia decesserat,; ; : priusquam ea cura decederet patribus,; so with dat., ; ; ; .—Poet.: incipit et longo Scyros decedere ponto,i. e. seems to flee before them,.—In the Aug. poets sometimes of the heavenly bodies, to go down, set: et sol crescentes decedens duplicat umbras,; so ; ; hence also of the day, to depart: te veniente die, te decedente canebat,; also of the moon,to wane,.
Trop.
De possessione, jure, sententia, fide, etc. (and since the Aug. per. with abl. alone; the reading ex jure suo,, is very doubtful), to depart from; to give up, resign, forego; to yield, to swerve from one's possession, station, duty, right, opinion, faith, etc.
With de: cogere aliquem de suis bonis decedere,; cf.: de hypothecis,; and de possessione,; de suo jure,; : qui de civitate decedere quam de sententia maluit,: de officio ac dignitate,: de foro decedere,to retire from public life,: de scena,to retire from the stage,; cf. impers.: de officio decessum,—
With abl. alone (so usually in Liv.): jure suo,: sententiā,: instituto vestro,: officio (opp. in fide atque officio pristino fore),; : fide,; ; : poema ... si paulum summo decessit, vergit ad imum,.—
Very rarely with ab: cum (senatus) nihil a superioribus continuorum annorum decretis decesserit,.—
Absol.: si quos equites decedentis nactus sum, supplicio adfeci, Asin. Pol. ap. 10, 32, 5.
De via, to depart, deviate from the right way: se nulla cupiditate inductum de via decessisse,: moleste ferre se de via decessisse,; so, viā dicendi,.
(acc. to no. I. B. 2) To give way, yield to another (i. e. to his will or superior advantages—very rare): vivere si recte nescis, decede peritis,: ubi non Hymetto Mella decedunt,are not inferior,.
(poet.) To avoid, shun, escape from (cf. I. B. 2 supra): nec serae meminit decedere nocti, to avoid the late night, i. e. the coldness of night, Varius ap. 6, 2, 20; ; : calori,.
To fall short of, degenerate from: de generis nobilitate,: a rebus gestis ejus et gloriae splendore, Justin. 6, 3, 8.
For the simple verb (v. cedo, no. I. 2), to go off, turn out, result in any manner: prospere decedentibus rebus,.

la:noun:decus.html:
dĕcus, ŏris, n.
Sanscr. daças, fame; Gr. δόξα; cf. decet
, any thing that ornaments, embellishes, adorns, honors, etc.;
ornament, grace, embellishment, splendor, glory, honor, dignity (class. and freq.; a favorite word with Cicero, in oratorical lang.).
In gen.
With gen.: hostium spolia, decora atque ornamenta fanorum,; cf.: senator populi Romani, splendor ordinis, decus atque ornamentum judiciorum,; so, too, decus ornamentumque senectutis,; : ut hominis decus ingenium, sic ingenii ipsius lumen est eloquentia,; cf. : ad decus et ad laudem civitatis,; cf. ; cf. also ; : dignitatem et decus sustinere, et saep.: O decus Phoebi et dapibus supremi Grata testudo Jovis,: lucidum caeli,: equitum Maecenas,; cf. and : electos juvenes simul et decus innuptarum, the ornaments, i. e. the most beautiful of the maidens, Catull. 64, 78 al.: castique decus servare pudoris,: oris,i. e. beauty,: decus Asteriae = Asteria decens or pulchra,.—
Absol.: haec omnia, quae habent speciem gloriae contemne ...; verum decus in virtute positum est,: divitiae, decus, gloria in oculis sita sunt!; cf. ; : regium,; cf. regale,: decus enitet ore,: superimpositum capiti,: (columnas) scenis decora alta futuris,: muliebre,i. e. chastity,: immemores decoris liventia pectora tundunt,i. e. of their bodily charms,: imperatori nobilitas, quae antea decori, invidiae esse,: vitis ut arboribus decori est, ut vitibus uvae,: Pilumno quos ipsa decus dedit,.—
Transf.
A deed of honor: tanti decoris testis,.—Esp., plur., decora, honorable achievements, valiant deeds: cum multa referret sua familiaeque decora,: militiae decora,: belli, (cf.: dedecora militiae,): Lacedaemonii vetera, Macedones praesentia decora intuebantur,.—
Renowned ancestors: inter nobiles, et longa decora praeferentes, novitas mea enituit?; .—
Esp., moral dignity, virtue, honor: cum quod decus antiqui summum bonum esse dixerunt, hic solum bonum dicat, etc., (for which, shortly before, solum bonum esse quod honestum esset): quos (sc. Epicureos) nisi redarguimus, omnis virtus, omne decus, omnis vera laus deserenda est,; so with honestas,; cf. ; : sed ei (sc. Semproniae) cariora semper omnia quam decus atque pudicitia fuit,; .

la:verb:declaro.html:
dē-clāro, āvi, ātum, 1,
v. a., to make clear, plain, evident (by disclosing, uncovering), to show, manifest, declare, etc., ἀποφαίνω (class.; most freq. in the trop. sense). For syn. cf.: monstro, demonstro, probo, confirmo, ostendo, ostento, significo, indico, defero; exsisto, appareo, eluceo. —
Lit.
In gen.: praesentiam saepe divisuam declarant, ut et apud Regillum.... Castor et Pollux ex equis pugnare visi sunt, Cic. N: D. 2, 2, 6: dentibus (cervorum) senecta declaratur,: ducis nave declarata suis,.—
In pub. law lang., t. t., to announce any one in public session as elected to an office (esp. that of consul), to declare or proclaim publicly: ejusdem hominis voce et declaratus consul et defensus, (for which shortly before, L. Murenam consulem renunciavi); cf. ; so consulem,; ; ; ; et saep.: declaratus rex Numa de templo descendit,; : consulem, praetorem,: tribunatum militarem,: : victorem magnā praeconis voce Cloanthum Declarat,. —
Trop., to make clear to the mind, to manifest, demonstrate, prove, show, explain: cum tot signis eadem natura declaret quid velit, tamen, etc.,.—Constr. with acc., acc. and inf., a relat. clause, or absol.
With acc.: volatibus avium et cantibus declarari res futuras putant,; cf. ; : ipsa consolatio litterarum tuarum declarat summam benevolentiam,: declarant gaudia vultu, * Catull. 64, 34 et saep.: propriam cujusque (generis juris civilis) vim definitione,: nullum (verbum) inveniri potest, quod magis idem declaret Latine, quod Graece ἡδονή, quam declarat voluptas, ; cf. in like manner of the meaning of words,; ; : verba ipsa per se declarant intellectum,: quae (litera C.) inversa mulierem declarat,.—
With acc. and inf.: hominem catum eum esse declaramus,; ; : quod plurimis locis perorationes nostrae voluisse nos atque animo contendisse declarant,; prooem. § 15 et saep.—
With a relative clause: quae cujusque ingenium ut sit declarat maxume,: ut matres familiae eorum sortibus et vaticinationibus declararent, utrum, etc.,: qui declaravit quanti me faceret,: cf. et saep.—
Absol.: ut ratio declarat eorum, qui, etc.,: declarant illae contiones,

senses: to be decent, suitable, seemly, or proper
la:verb:decet.html:
dĕcet, cuit, 2,
v. impers. [Sanscr. dacas, fame; Gr. δοκέω, to seem, think; Lat. decus, dignus]. It is seemly, comely, becoming,; it beseems, behooves, is fitting, suitable, proper (for syn. v. debeo init.): decere quasi aptum esse consentaneumque tempori et personae,; cf. also nunc quid aptum sit, hoc est, quid maxime deceat in oratione videamus, (very freq. and class.; not in Caes.).—Constr., with nom. or inf. of the thing, and with acc.; less freq. with dat. of the pers.; sometimes absol.
With nom. rei
and acc. pers.: Ph. Quin me aspice et contempla, ut haec (sc. vestis) me decet. Sc. Virtute formae id evenit, te ut deceat, quicquid habeas, ; cf.: quem decet muliebris ornatus, quem incessus psaltriae, Cic. Clod. fragm. 5, p. 105 ed. Beier: te toga picta decet,; ; ; and nec habitus triumphalis feminas deceat,; cf.: omnis Aristippum color decuit,: intonsus crinis deum,; cf.: neglecta decet multas coma,; et saep.: id maxime quemque decet, quod est cujusque maxime suum,: quod omnes et semper et ubique decet,: non si quid Pholoen satis, Et te, Chlori, decet, et saep.: qui flexus deceat miserationem,: civitatem quis deceat status, et saep.—In plur.: quem tenues decuere togae nitidique capilli,: te non citharae decent,: alba decent Cererem: vestes Cerealibus albas Sumite,; et saep.: nec velle experiri, quam se aliena deceant,; : illa quoque diversa bonum virum decent, et saep.: duo verba uni apposita ne versum quidem decuerint,.—
Without acc. pers.: nihil est difficilius quam quid deceat videre,; cf.: quid deceat et quid aptum sit personis,: casus singularis magis decuit,, 20; et saep.: idem fere in omni genere causarum et proderit et decebit,; cf. .—In plur.: ubi lepos, joci, risus, vinum, ebrietas decent,: cum magna pars est exhausta orationis, pene omnia decent,; ; et saep. —
With dat.: istuc facinus nostro generi non decet,: certa est ratio quae deceat philosopho, Apul. ; ; cf. infra. —
With inf.
and acc. pers.: non te mihi irasci decet,: hanc maculam nos decet effugere,: oratorem irasci minime decet,; ; ; so freq. with inf. pass.: specimen naturae capi debet ex optima quaque natura,: mortalin' decuit violari vulnere divum?; . —
Without acc.: injusta ab justis impetrare non decet,: exemplis grandioribus decuit uti,; : nunc decet caput impedire myrto: nunc et in umbrosis Fauno decet immolare lucis,; ; .—
With dat.: decet tantae majestati eas servare leges, quibus, etc.,: ita uti liberali esse ingenio decet,: prima certe pensari decet populo utrum, etc.,.
Absol.
with acc. pers.: ita ut vos decet,; cf.: facis, ut te decet,; : ita uti fortes decet milites,; cf.: : illum decet, et saep.—
Without case: eia haud sic decet,; cf. : fecisti ut decuerat,: minus severe quam decuit,: velata parte oris, quia sic decebat,it was becoming,: nihil aliter ac deceat,: perge; decet, et saep.—
With dat.: ita nobis decet,; : locum editiorem quam victoribus decebat, (.)— Hence, dĕcens, entis, P. a. (freq. in Hor., Ov., and post-Aug. prose, esp. Quint.; not in Verg.; in Cic. once adverbially, and cf. decentia), seemly, becoming, decent, proper, fit: amictus,; cf.: decentior amictus,; and sinus (togae) decentissimus,: ornatus,: motus,; ; cf.: corporis decens et accommodatus orationi motus,; and allevatio atque contractio humerorum,: decentissimum sponsalium genus, et saep.: quid verum atque decens,: decentius erit servare pudorem,; cf. 8, 6, 6.—
Esp. of corporeal fitness and symmetry, regularly, symmetrically, handsomely shaped; well-formed; noble: forma,; cf.: habitus decentior quam sublimior,: facies,: malae,: Venus,; cf.: Cynthia, (5, 8, 52 M.): Gratiae,: (Paullus) et nobilis et decens,: pulcher et decens toto corpore, Suct. Dom. 18; cf. : sumptis decentior armis Minerva,; et saep.—Adv.: decenter (acc. to no. 1), becomingly, decently, properly, fitly: fictis nominibus decenter uti,; cf.: fieri,: singula quaeque locum teneant sortita decenter,; cf.: maesta,.—Comp.: ; —Sup., a false reading for diligentissime, .

dĕcus, ŏris, n.

Epicureos) nisi redarguimus, omnis virtus, omne decus, omnis vera laus deserenda est,; so with honestas,; cf. ; : sed ei (sc. Semproniae) cariora semper omnia quam decus atque pudicitia fuit,; .

la:adj:decorus.html:
dĕcōrus, a, um, adj.
decor
, Gr. εὐπρεπής.
Becoming, fitting, seemly, proper, suitable, decorous (class.).
With dat.: QVAE QVOIQVE DIVO DECORAE GRATAEQVE SINT HOSTIAE PROVIDENTO,: color albus praecipue decorus deo est,: quod virginitati decorum,; ; cf. ib. § 104, and 11,

1, 33 al.: decorum erat tum ipsis capessere pugnam ducibus,; cf. . —*

With abl. (after the analogy of dignus): (facinora puerilia) neque te decora neque tuis virtutibus, (cf. ).—*
With ad (after the analogy of aptus, accommodatus, etc.): nos auri venas invenimus et ad usum aptas et ad ornatum decoras,.—
With pro: decorum pro causa ratus,.—(ε) Absol.: decorus est senis sermo, quietus et remissus,; cf.: vox et actio,: silentium, et saep.: nihil nisi quod honestum decorumque sit admirari,: omnino si quicquam est decorum, nihil est profecto magis, quam aequabilitas universae vitae,; : actuariis minutis Patras accedere ... non satis visum est decorum,; so with a subject-clause, : dulce et decorum est pro patria mori,; (opp. turpe); cf. —
Subst.: dĕ-cōrum, i, n., in Cic. for the Gr. πρέπον, that which is seemly, suitable; seemliness, fitness, propriety, decorum (for which Quint. uses decor; cf.: decus init.): ut in vita, sic in oratione nihil est difficilius quam quid deceat videre. Πρέπον appellant hoc Graeci: nos dicamus sane decorum; ; cf.: id, quod Graece πρέπον dicitur, decorum dici Latine potest, etc., ; cf. ; .—Plur.: vota pro reditu ejus et alia decora,: plura tribuere,.
Absol., decorated, ornamented, adorned; elegant, fine, beautiful, handsome (not so in Cic.; but freq. in the poets and historians, esp. in Hor. and Tacit.): delubra deum, * ; cf.: aedes,; and: supplicationes et alia decora,: galeae ensesque,: insigne clipei,: arma,: membra juventae,; cf.: oculi,: pectus,: os,: facies,; : caput,: juventa,: genus,: palaestra,noble, skilful,: verba,; : temporibus Augusti dicendis non defuere decora ingenia,.—Sup.: Zeus decorissimus, Apul. Mag. 4, p. 276, 4.—
With abl., adorned with any thing; shining, beautiful with any thing: ductores ostro decori,; cf. : Phoebus fulgente arcu,: Bacchus aureo cornu,: Medi pharetrā,: dea formāque armisque,: satis decorus etiam Graeca facundia,.— With ab: voces decorae ab aspectu,.Adv.: dĕcōrē.
(Acc. to no. I.) Suitably, properly, decorously: ut ea si non decore, at quam minime indecore facere possimus,; cf. ; ; —*
(acc. to no. II.), elegantly, charmingly, beautifully: formata d. Jovis species, Cic. poët. Div. 1, 12, 20 (cf. above, decora delubra deum).

Esp., milit. t. t., to go through military exercises or manœuvres, to advance rapidly, to charge, skirmish, etc.: pedites decurrendo signa sequi et servare ordines docuit,while performing evolutions,; cf. ; ; : ex montibus in vallem,; cf.: ex omnibus partibus,: ex superiore loco,: ex Capitolio in hostem,: ab arce,: inde (sc. a Janiculo), et saep.: incredibili celeritate ad flumen,.—Pass. impers.: quinto (die) iterum in armis de cursum est,.—
